old.note_beginner: The soil water mold behind this rot builds up in ground that stays wet, so drainage under and around the tree leaves less of it there to be thrown onto the fruit when it rains. In areas with dry falls the disease is uncommon to begin with.
old.note_seasoned: Drainage lowers the inoculum available to splash, since the organism is soil-borne and its numbers track how wet the ground stays. It acts on the source rather than on the fruit, and it counts for most in wet-winter regions; where fall and winter stay dry the disease is uncommon.

old.note_beginner: Lay mulch under the tree to cut down on splashing. The rot reaches the fruit when rain throws soil up onto it, so a layer between the soil and the low-hanging fruit takes away the route.
old.note_seasoned: Mulch interrupts the splash pathway from soil to low-hanging rind, which is the transmission step this disease depends on. It goes down ahead of the cool wet season rather than in response to symptoms, and it is among the more dependable cultural controls here.

old.note_beginner: Pick the low-hanging fruit early. Mature fruit near the ground is what this rot takes, so getting it off the tree before the cool wet weather arrives removes the target.
old.note_seasoned: Harvesting low fruit promptly takes mature, susceptible rind out of the splash zone ahead of the cool, wet fall and winter period when infection occurs. The low position on the tree is both the diagnostic clue and where this step applies.

old.note_beginner: Pick off and throw away any rotted fruit right away rather than leaving it on the tree or lying underneath. The decay carries on in storage, so a rotted fruit put away with the sound ones can spread it there.
old.note_seasoned: Prompt removal and disposal of rotted fruit limits carryover, since the decay continues in storage and one infected fruit put away with sound ones extends it. Take the culls out of the planting rather than leaving them under the canopy.

old.note_beginner: Where brown rot keeps coming back in a wet-winter area, a copper spray on the lower canopy and the low fruit before the rains start is the standard preventive. It protects rather than cures, so getting the timing ahead of the wet weather is what makes it work. Copper is toxic to fish, builds up in the soil, and can burn foliage above the label rate, so follow the label and keep spray and runoff out of drains and waterways.
old.note_seasoned: A copper application to the lower canopy and fruit ahead of the rainy season is the accepted preventive where the disease recurs in wet-winter regions; it is protective, so it has to precede the infection period to buy anything.
